German Steel Sector Reflects on 2018 Credit Freeze and its Aftermath

In 2018, Germany’s steel industry faced its most severe financial crisis in decades, triggered by a sudden credit freeze that rippled through the sector. As steelmakers sought to refinance existing debt amid tightening global credit markets, several mid-sized firms, such as Westfalenstahl AG and RuhrMetall GmbH, found themselves unable to secure short-term financing. The freeze led to a series of defaults and forced restructuring across the industry, causing widespread uncertainty and operational disruptions.

At the peak of the crisis in late 2018, the German Steel Federation (Deutscher Stahlverband) reported that over 30 percent of domestic steel producers were at risk of insolvency. Orders for structural and specialty steel products dropped by nearly 18 percent in the fourth quarter, according to the industry group. “The abrupt halt in credit availability struck at the core of our sector’s stability,” recalled Dr. Markus Feldmann, then president of the federation. “Firms suddenly faced cash-flow shortages, putting wages and investment projects in jeopardy.”

The credit freeze was exacerbated by plummeting steel prices on the European spot market, which fell by 22 percent between September and December 2018, according to figures from the Hanover Commodities Exchange. As banks tightened lending standards, even healthy firms struggled to roll over their financing or fund inventory. “We had to suspend production at two of our mills for several weeks,” said a spokesperson for Westfalenstahl AG at the time. “Without access to working capital, we simply could not operate at normal capacity.”

Trade unions responded with urgent calls for government intervention to secure jobs. “Thousands of livelihoods were on the line,” said Annegret Schulte, regional chair of IG Metall North Rhine-Westphalia. “It was only through coordinated action between lenders, government, and unions that a wave of bankruptcies was averted.”

In the months that followed, restructuring agreements and emergency credit lines helped stabilize the industry. While no major disruptions are reported today, the 2018 crisis remains a cautionary tale for Germany’s steel producers about the risks of overreliance on short-term financing and volatile credit conditions.
